source: Bala and Goyal (1998) Learning from Neighbours, Rev. Econ. Studies 65:595-621 (read as the July 1996 working-paper version)
finding: Founding result, but a different model from the Zollman two-armed bandit. Extra information links can lock a society into a worse action. A small 'Royal Family' of agents seen by everyone can push all agents off the better, uncertain action after a run of bad luck, and then no new information is produced.
numbers: Example: integer-line society, each agent sees both neighbours plus a Royal Family of 5. With positive probability all five royal agents give a negative first draw, every agent switches to the safe action at t=2, and learning stops. Simulations (N=100, Royal Family size 1 to 10, Bernoulli and Normal payoffs): probability of incomplete learning can be as high as 0.2 and rises roughly with Royal Family size for small sizes.
quote: more information links can make the society worse o[ff]
limits: Theory plus small simulations only. Not the Zollman speed-for-reliability trade-off: the lock-in comes from a hub of publicly seen agents and from prior beliefs that are not dispersed. The paper says it is not a full characterisation.
agent_relevance: Direct analogue of one shared scratchpad or one leader answer that every attempt reads: a few early negative draws can make all attempts abandon the better path. Supports G4: no shared hub in the first pass.

source: Bala and Goyal (1998/1996 version) ring society and integration simulations
finding: Without a Royal Family, in a ring where each agent sees two neighbours, the chance of incomplete learning falls quickly as the society grows. Integration between two groups is inversely related to the chance that both groups keep different actions (diversity).
numbers: Ring of N agents, Bernoulli and Normal payoffs: log probability of incomplete learning is near-linear in N, R-squared above 0.99 (Bernoulli) and 0.94 to 0.98 (Normal). Diversity simulations: two groups, k=9, 20 agents total; diversity falls as the integration parameter rises.
limits: Figures read only through their text description, curves not read. Society sizes are large relative to an agent run.
agent_relevance: Local, sparse structure plus many independent starts protects learning. Supports many separate attempts over a few heavily shared ones.

source: Mason and Watts (2012) Collaborative learning in networks, PNAS 109:764-769
finding: Large human experiment (Wildcat Wells, a 15-round search for hidden oil on a 2D map). Networked groups beat the same number of independent searchers. Independence did not buy better exploration.
numbers: 256 web experiments, groups of 16 players, 8 network topologies, 232 networked sessions. When at least one player found the main peak: networked 68 points vs independent 39 (t=92.5). When nobody found it: networked 40.5 vs independent 32. Probability that someone found the peak was marginally higher for independent searchers but not significant.
limits: Mechanical Turk workers, 15 rounds, each player saw exactly 3 collaborators and was not told the network. One main peak plus local maxima. Smooth 2D space where any point is reachable from any other.
agent_relevance: Human evidence that the independence advantage does not appear by default. Sharing helps when a good solution can be copied and checked cheaply. The agent needs a rule for when sharing is safe (a checkable result), not blanket isolation.

source: Mason and Watts (2012) efficient vs inefficient networks (test of Lazer-Friedman and Zollman)
finding: Failed to reproduce the 'inefficient networks win' result in humans. Short average path length gave higher scores. Clustered, slow networks led players to copy each other more, not explore more.
numbers: Regression of score on average path length: beta = -4.63, P about 0.01 (shorter paths better). The peak was found in 138 of 232 sessions (59.5%). Time for news of the peak to reach a node equalled its path length in 71% of cases. Copying more likely when 2 or more neighbours exploited the same spot (z=38.9); more clustering meant neighbours more likely on the same spot (z=15.96). Peak-finding rate: efficient networks slightly higher, not significant.
quote: we find no evidence to support the hypothesized superiority of inefficient networks
limits: Authors blame simulation assumptions about copying, not the landscape (theirs was designed to favour slow networks). Path-length range was only a factor of 1.5. Human copying of a visible neighbour over 15 rounds differs from a Bayesian bandit agent.
agent_relevance: The effect of topology depends on how agents copy. For an LLM, test its copying rule directly: does it anchor on a visible earlier answer? (see d12, d16).

source: Derex and Boyd (2016) Partial connectivity increases cultural accumulation within groups, PNAS 113:2982-2987
finding: Human lab support for the isolation benefit in a cumulative-innovation task. Fully connected groups converged early on one path and never combined two. Partly isolated subgroups found both and recombined them.
numbers: Groups of 6, 72 trials, 12 replicate groups per condition. Third-level innovation A3: 50% (fully connected) vs 91.7% (partial). B3: 33.3% vs 66.7%. Both A3 and B3: 0% vs 58.3%. Every partial group that reached both made 4th-level innovations. Fully connected groups reached their best score after about 35 trials. Participants adopted a newly shown ingredient within two trials in almost 70% of cases. Fully connected groups did better in the short run.
quote: partially connected groups produce more diverse solutions
limits: Small N (12 groups per arm), one lab, a 6-ingredient puzzle built to need recombination. Acquisition of traits was easy; authors say real fragmentation brings cultural loss, so an optimum exists. Isolation was temporary (first 36 trials), then contact.
agent_relevance: Best match for the schema: isolate first, then merge. It supports staged isolation then one combine step (S3 then merge), not permanent isolation. The benefit appears when solutions can be recombined.

source: Becker, Brackbill, Centola (2017) Network dynamics of social influence in the wisdom of crowds, PNAS 114:E5070-E5076
finding: Counter-evidence to the strong 'influence hurts' reading. Estimates became far less diverse after sharing, yet in decentralised networks the group got more accurate. In centralised networks the group answer moved toward the hub's belief, helping or hurting depending on whether the hub was right.
numbers: 13 trials per network condition, 3 rounds. Decentralised: SD of estimates fell 43% between round 1 and 3 (P<0.001); average individual error fell 23%; median-estimate error fell from 0.76 to 0.67 SD (12%). Centralised: group mean and median got less accurate when the central node pointed away from the truth (n=13, P<0.01) and more accurate when toward it (n=12).
limits: Numeric estimation, not search for a hard-to-find option. Few trials. Diversity loss was harmless there because errors were unbiased noise, the opposite of a rare correct answer.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: isolation matters when the correct answer is rare and a minority holds it, not when errors are symmetric noise. For numeric guesses, one limited share round can help. A hub (strong first answer) is the risk.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang, Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context? (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: Closest LLM test to a real bandit, but for a single agent. Without outside help, LLMs fail to explore: they lock onto an arm and never try the best one again. This is the Bala-Goyal failure inside one head.
numbers: Multi-armed bandit, K=5 arms, gap 0.2 (hard instance), T=100 (main) and T=200, N=10 to 40 replicates. GPT-4 with the basic prompt at temperature 0: suffix failure (best arm never chosen late in the run) in more than 60% of replicates. Only one configuration in all (GPT-4, chain-of-thought, externally summarised history as sufficient statistics) explored well. Others show suffix failures or uniform-like failure.
limits: One agent; no network, no sharing. GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama2 only. Stationary Bernoulli arms. Says nothing about independent vs shared attempts.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open: nobody has run independent vs shared LLM agents on a real bandit. This paper shows why it matters: one in-context agent already acts like a dense network that collapses after early bad luck. Independent restarts are the cheap fix; an external summary of results helps.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: Best evidence on gaps 2, 3 and 9. On easy questions, sequential revision of one's own answer beats independent parallel samples. On hard questions, independent parallel samples or search win, and a mix is best.
numbers: MATH, PaLM 2-S* based revision model. Ratio sweep at 128 generations with a verifier: easier questions reach best accuracy with full sequential compute; harder questions have an interior best ratio (a balance of sequential and parallel). Compute-optimal revisions can beat best-of-N using up to 4x less test-time compute. At small budgets more sequential is better; at higher budgets there is an ideal ratio.
quote: easy questions benefit more from sequential revisions
limits: Revision model was fine-tuned for revising (data built from 64 parallel samples, up to 4 wrong answers in context). Selection used a trained verifier or majority. One benchmark, one model family. Untuned models handle earlier wrong answers badly (see d11, d12).
agent_relevance: Answer to gaps 2 and 3 for math: hardness favours independent attempts; ease favours revising. The schema can route by estimated difficulty: easy items get a revision pass, hard ones fresh independent attempts. Needs a difficulty signal such as agreement among first samples.

source: Snell et al. (2024) sequential vs parallel under majority and verifier selection
finding: Averaged over difficulty, for the tuned revision model, generating answers in sequence narrowly beat generating them in parallel, with both majority vote and verifier selection. The split by difficulty matters more than the average.
numbers: Figure 6 right: sequential majority and sequential best-of-N weighted both narrowly above parallel at matched generation count (read from text; narrow gap). Mixed strategy best at large budgets.
limits: Narrow average difference; depends on the fine-tuned reviser. Not token-exact: revisions carry earlier answers in context, so each call costs more tokens than a fresh call.
agent_relevance: Do not conclude revise is better or fresh is better without a difficulty split.

source: Olausson et al. (2023/2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation? (ICLR 2024)
finding: At equal token budget, repairing a failed program is often no better than drawing fresh programs. The best use of budget is more diverse initial samples, not more repairs.
numbers: Code Llama, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 on HumanEval and APPS. Budget measured in tokens (pass@t). Gains from self-repair are modest, vary a lot between subsets and are sometimes absent; at small budgets repair gains are marginal or non-existent. More initial programs at fixed repairs gave consistent gains for all models; more repairs at fixed initial programs gave marginal gains at high budgets and sometimes lower performance at low budgets. A stronger model giving the feedback raised repair gains a lot.
quote: the most important factor ... is the diversity of the base samples
limits: Code with unit tests as the error signal; repair sees failed code plus an error message, a richer signal than a blind revision. Older models. Paper says it is hard to predict when repair wins; stronger models repair easy tasks well but also solve them fresh.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 in code: at equal tokens, fresh independent attempts beat revising; revision pays only when feedback is good. Supports G4: fresh attempts first, use test feedback only if a real test exists.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Without an outside signal, asking a model to revise its own reasoning answer usually does not help and often hurts. Debate gains over a single answer are matched by plain voting with the same number of responses.
numbers: GPT-3.5 self-correction: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7 over rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after round 1. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. Self-consistency on GSM8K: standard 76.7; 3, 6, 9 responses 82.5, 85.3, 88.2; the paper reports debate with equal response counts at or below it.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback
limits: 2023 models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2) and prompts like review-and-fix; 2025-26 reasoning models may self-correct better. Oracle-label self-correction does help, but is not usable.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: for reasoning questions with no external check, fresh attempt plus vote is safer than revising. Revise only with an outside checker.

source: Madaan et al. (2025) Rethinking thinking tokens: LLMs as improvement operators (Parallel-Distill-Refine)
finding: Sequential refinement beats one long chain at matched sequential tokens, and parallel drafts distilled into a short workspace do better still. Putting wrong candidates into the workspace hurts a lot, an anchoring effect that depends on the model's self-verification.
numbers: AIME 2024, o3-mini, effective budget 49k tokens (16k per call): long CoT 76.9, sequential refinement 81.5, PDR 86.7. Oracle workspace test (3 rounds, 16, 8, 4 drafts, top-2): admitting only incorrect candidates causes large drops; only correct candidates lifts above random-k. Drop larger for o3-mini than gemini-2.5-flash. Trained 8B model: PDR gains +11% AIME 2024 and +9% AIME 2025.
limits: Budget Bseq counts only the accepted path; tokens in unused parallel drafts are excluded, so PDR uses more total compute. Verifiable math only. Oracle conditions use ground truth, not available in practice.
agent_relevance: Evidence for a limited-visibility design: parallel independent drafts, then one distilled, bounded merge step. Gap 9: PDR is a break-even candidate. Caveat: counts latency tokens, not total.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Towards a science of scaling agent systems
finding: Across many configurations, independent multi-agent runs without checking amplify errors, and gains depend on task structure and on how weak the single agent already is.
numbers: Error amplification: Independent 17.2x vs Centralized 4.4x. Change vs single agent: BrowseComp-Plus independent -35%; Finance Agent +57% to +80.8% across multi-agent variants; PlanCraft -39% to -70%; SWE-bench Verified independent -14.9%; Terminal-Bench independent +1.7%. Capability ceiling: where a single agent exceeds about 45%, more agents give negative returns (beta -0.236, p=0.004). Decentralised +9.2% on dynamic web navigation. Communication overhead: Independent 58%, Decentralised 263%, Centralized 285%, Hybrid 515%.
limits: Their Independent arm aggregates with a fixed rule and no cross-check at fixed total budget; it is not independent attempts with a verifier or vote. Commercial models, agentic tasks with tools.
agent_relevance: Independent parallel attempts are not free wins: they need a check at the end (central validation cut amplification to 4.4x). Where one try already works (above about 45%), do not add attempts.

source: Zheng, Yang, Qu, Wang, Jeong (2026) Absorbing state phase transitions in multi-agent search: negative-result sharing
finding: Gap 4 mostly answered for communication quality, not for token cost. When every experiment verdict, including failures, is passed automatically, agents get close to the theory. When agents choose what to share, they under-report negative results and need many more links.
numbers: Free communication (Table 3, six task seeds, three environments): negative findings disclosed 51.5%/53.2% (Qwen3.5-4B Team/Indiv), 36.1%/35.4% (Qwen3.5-9B), 72.5%/69.1% (GPT-5.4 Nano), 84.3%/82.4% (GPT-6 Luna); positive findings 66.1%/65.6%, 49.8%/49.0%, 80.3%/75.5%, 84.0%/82.5%. Misreported outcomes under 1.2%. Excess critical degree (free vs auto) correlates r = -0.91 with the report rate. Free minus Team-Auto, synthetic task: Qwen3.5-9B +9.4, GPT-6 Luna about 0.
limits: Synthetic hidden-configuration search plus two physics-style tasks, small and new models. No token or cost accounting in the text. Whether negative sharing fixes herding on open reasoning problems is untested.
agent_relevance: Cheap fix to try: force a short structured 'tried and failed' line from every attempt into a shared board, only after each attempt is finished so the first answer stays independent. Token cost remains an open measurement.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) reasoning effort and sampling temperature
finding: Gaps 5 and 7, partial. More reasoning effort makes agents pick the same promising paths, which cuts exploration and raises the communication needed. Higher temperature widens candidate choice; lowering it mattered mostly on one task where the clue is obvious.
numbers: Unique literals tested fell from 25.5 to 11.3 (TCAS) and 14.2 to 8.8 (physics) with higher effort on GPT-6 Luna; individual success equal or higher. Temperature 0.2 vs 1: higher temperature made agents select a wider range and reap communication benefits. T=0.2 raised the critical degree noticeably only for GPT-5.4-Nano on the physical mechanism task, where adding a damping term is obvious from the data.
limits: T=0.2 not available for GPT-6 Luna. Authors say task obviousness may explain it: with an easy clue, herding is harmless. No test of the Kummerfeld-Zollman reverse effect; the closest is that high temperature plus communication was beneficial.
agent_relevance: Raising reasoning effort shrinks the diversity of independent samples, so vary seeds, prompts or strategies rather than rely on temperature alone. Weak hint for gap 2: herding costs most when the signal is hard to see.

source: Jiang et al. (2025/2026) Artificial Hivemind: the open-ended homogeneity of language models
finding: Independent samples from one model, and from different models, are far more alike than they look. Aggressive sampling settings do not remove it.
numbers: 50 responses per query on 100 open-ended queries (INFINITY-CHAT100). Under top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0 the average within-prompt pairwise embedding similarity typically exceeds 0.8 (a random pairing sits at 0.1 to 0.2). With min-p 0.1 and temperature 2.0, 81% of response pairs still exceed 0.7. Across models, average similarity 0.71 to 0.82; DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82, DeepSeek-V3 vs gpt-4o 0.81. Dataset 26K queries, 31,250 human annotations.
limits: Open-ended generation, not reasoning with one correct answer. Embedding similarity (text-embedding-3-small) is a proxy. No persona-prompt test in what I read, so the persona question (gap 5) stays open here.
agent_relevance: Voting over independent samples counts correlated votes. Diversity must be injected structurally (different strategies, different models); temperature does not do it. Cross-model ensembles are less independent than expected.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Verbalized sampling: how to mitigate mode collapse and unlock LLM diversity
finding: A training-free prompt that asks the model to list several answers with probabilities restores diversity better than direct prompting, on creative and dialogue tasks; stronger models gain more.
numbers: Creative writing: diversity 1.6 to 2.1 times direct prompting (abstract). Factual accuracy and safety reported as not reduced. Cause given: typicality bias in preference data.
limits: Read the abstract and introduction text only, not the per-task tables. Creative, simulation and synthetic-data tasks; not shown to raise correctness on hard reasoning.
agent_relevance: A candidate way to get diverse attempts from one model in one call. Gap 5 'prompt differences restore it' is supported for open tasks only; untested for math or search.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence improves self-consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: Gap 8: confidence-weighted voting beats plain majority at equal sample counts. Weighted by the model's own confidence, it reaches the same accuracy with fewer samples.
numbers: Nine models, four datasets. Average reduction in required reasoning paths over 40%; with P(True) confidence the cost reduction is 41% at a budget of 5 samples and 46% at 10. Outperforms self-consistency in nearly all configurations. Gemma2-9B on MATH: 73% cost reduction at one point (Figure 1).
limits: Same-model self-confidence, not an external verifier; no head-to-head against a trained verifier. It addresses voting among independent samples, not the expert-dilution result of Pappu et al.
agent_relevance: A cheap upgrade to plain voting inside the independent-attempt design. Does not settle whether a lone expert is rescued from a wrong majority.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large language monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Gaps 8 and 9. Independent sampling keeps finding correct answers far past 100 samples, but majority vote and reward models stop improving. Only a real verifier turns coverage into accuracy.
numbers: MATH with Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000; majority voting or reward-model selection only 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range. SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2: 15.9% at 1 sample to 56% at 250 samples with a perfect verifier. Voting and reward models plateau beyond about 100 samples.
limits: The plateau depends on task and model. Verifier cases are code and proofs. The 8-sample plateau noted earlier for MacNet is not the same setting.
agent_relevance: With a checkable result, extra independent attempts keep paying; without one, put budget into a verifier or one limited merge step instead of more votes.

source: Mayo-Wilson, Zollman, Danks (2011) The independence thesis; (2013) Wisdom of crowds versus groupthink
finding: Not opened. Crossref confirms both titles (Philosophy of Science 2011, DOI 10.1086/661777; Int. J. Game Theory 2013, DOI 10.1007/s00182-012-0329-7). The archive guess URL returned an HTML page, not a PDF; the Zollman site link was 404.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Metadata only. Gap 6 for this paper stays open.
agent_relevance: Needs a read of the theorem statements before any 'independence thesis' claim is used.
